---
title: "Caching"
---

Every fetch is cached, and the cache is the reason a re-run is cheap.

## What is kept

| Path | What | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data/raw/items/<id>.html` | Skemman item page | ~30 KB each |
| `data/raw/pdf_text/<id>.txt` | First pages of the PDF, as plain text | ~5 KB each |
| `data/raw/pdfs/<id>.pdf` | Only with `--keep-pdf` | megabytes |

`<id>` is the Skemman handle suffix throughout, so `data/raw/pdf_text/10688.txt`,
`data/raw/items/10688.html` and <https://skemman.is/handle/1946/10688> are the same thesis.

## Why text and not the PDF

A master's thesis averages about 7 MB and the largest seen is over 500 MB. Keeping the
PDFs for one university's master's theses costs around 12 GB; keeping the first eight
pages as text costs about 20 MB.

The text is all the parser reads, so nothing is lost — and the PDF can always be fetched
again from Skemman if you need it.

## The page-count marker

The first line of each text file is a marker holding the PDF's page count:

```
%%PAGES	106
Mid-Holocene eruptive activity in the Hekla volcanic system
...
```

Without it, deleting the PDF would throw away how long the thesis was. With it, the number
survives in five bytes.

## Improving the parser costs nothing

Because the text is cached, a better parser can be run over everything already harvested
without a single request:

```bash
duckdb thesis.db -c "drop table thesis_titlepage"
skemman titlepage-load
```

That re-parses at roughly 75 theses a second, against 0.4 a second when fetching.

## What is not cached

A PDF that cannot be read is **not** cached, so a truncated download is retried next time
rather than being silently skipped forever.

A PDF that reads but yields no text — a scan — *is* cached, with its page count. That is a
real answer, not a failure.
